name: Replayability
summary: The ability to reprocess historical data or events deterministically to rebuild state or fix a bug.
description: Replayability is the capacity to re-run past inputs through the pipeline and arrive at the same — or a corrected — result. It underpins bug fixes (rerun after fixing transform logic), disaster recovery (rebuild a corrupted downstream from source), and reprocessing (adopt a new schema retroactively). It depends on retaining an immutable, replayable source of truth (a durable event log or immutable raw/bronze layer) and on transforms being deterministic. It weakens sharply when the source is mutated in place, logs have short retention, or transforms depend on non-reproducible external state.

mechanisms.name: Event log retention
mechanisms.note: Retaining the raw event log (or compacted tiers) long enough lets consumers rewind to any offset and replay history through updated logic.

mechanisms.name: Immutable raw / bronze layer
mechanisms.note: Landing source data append-only and never mutating it in place preserves a faithful record that any downstream layer can be rebuilt from.

mechanisms.name: Time-travel snapshots
mechanisms.note: Table formats keep prior snapshots/versions so a replay can read the data exactly as it was at a point in time rather than as it is now.

mechanisms.name: Deterministic transforms
mechanisms.note: Pure, side-effect-free transformations that depend only on their inputs guarantee that replaying the same source yields the same output.

mechanisms.name: Reprocessing from source
mechanisms.note: Reset consumer offsets or re-read raw partitions to feed history through a new pipeline version, materializing a fresh corrected state.

manifestations.statement: Replay is the defining idea: retain the log, reset offsets to zero, and re-run the (new) stream job to rebuild all derived state from history — no separate batch path needed.
A durable, retained event log lets any consumer rewind and reprocess past events through updated handlers, making it natural to rebuild a projection or onboard a new service against full history.
The immutable log plus versioned table snapshots means history can be replayed into corrected tables, and time-travel lets consumers verify against the state as it stood at any commit.
Bronze is retained immutable raw, so silver and gold can be fully recomputed from history after a logic fix; time-travel on the table format supports point-in-time replays.
Raw events are kept append-only at volume, so aggregations and sessionization can be replayed from source whenever the enrichment or attribution logic changes.
Snapshot history and time-travel make it straightforward to replay transforms against the data as it existed at a prior snapshot and rebuild downstream tables deterministically.
The batch layer exists precisely to recompute authoritative views from immutable master data, so replaying corrected logic over full history is a first-class, designed-for operation.
Telemetry retained in the log and raw store can be replayed to rebuild aggregates, though extreme fleet volumes often force shorter log retention, capping how far back a full replay can reach.
Everything lands immutable schema-on-read, so raw is always available to reprocess; replay determinism is only as good as the ad-hoc jobs reading it, which are not always reproducible.
If raw loads are retained, dbt models replay deterministically via full-refresh; replay is bounded by how much raw history the ingestion tool kept rather than by the transforms.
Staging preserves source-shaped data so marts can be rebuilt on demand, but if staging itself is incrementally overwritten, replaying beyond retained history is not possible.

Insert-only satellites keep full history so information marts can be recomputed from the vault, giving strong within-warehouse replay; replaying the ingestion of a source itself still depends on that source's retention.

Point-in-time-correct offline stores let feature logic be replayed over history to regenerate training sets, but reproducing the exact online serving state at a past instant is harder and often approximate.

Transform-before-load often discards or overwrites source detail in the governed target, so replaying corrected logic is only possible if raw extracts were separately retained — frequently they were not.
CDC upserts mutate the target to mirror current source state, so unless change events are archived, past states are overwritten and cannot be replayed — you see now, not as-of.

Type-1 dimensions overwrite prior attribute values in place, sacrificing the ability to replay history for those attributes; only Type-2 tracked columns and retained staging support a faithful replay.

Replaying means re-pushing history into SaaS destinations, which mutate live business state (emails, records); it is rarely safe to replay for correctness and there is no source-of-truth log to rewind.
Federation reads remote sources live and stores nothing, so there is no retained history under its control to replay; you can only re-query whatever the underlying systems currently hold.

tradeoffs.title: Cost efficiency
tradeoffs.note: Replay requires retaining raw events or the immutable event log for long windows, and that extended storage footprint drives up ongoing storage bills.

tradeoffs.title: Throughput
tradeoffs.note: Reprocessing historical data competes with live workloads for the same compute and I/O, so replay runs throttle or slow current ingestion unless capacity is over-provisioned.

tradeoffs.title: Maintainability
tradeoffs.note: Every transform must remain deterministic and version-pinned so a replay reproduces identical results, adding discipline around versioning code, config, and reference data.

tradeoffs.title: Operational complexity
tradeoffs.note: Coordinating replays without corrupting downstream state requires careful sequencing, watermark handling, and isolation from live outputs.
